text: Here is a string of six bracket characters to check.
Beside it, an empty stack will grow upward as we scan.
Every opening bracket we see gets pushed onto that stack.
Every closing bracket must match whatever sits on top.
A mismatch at any point means the string is invalid.
The first character is an opening curly brace: push it.
Next is an opening square bracket, pushed right on top.
Then an opening round bracket, also pushed onto the stack.
A closing round bracket arrives and matches the top: pop.
A closing square bracket comes next, matching the new top.
Finally a closing curly brace matches the very last item.
The stack is empty and every bracket found its match.
A stack works because the most recent opener closes first.
Now try a trickier string with just four characters.
An opening round bracket arrives, so we push it.
An opening square bracket follows, pushed right on top.
A closing round bracket appears, but the top is square.
They do not match, so the string is invalid right here.
Unlike the first string, this one fails at the very first clash.
We have now seen both a clean match and a real mismatch.
Both checks needed just one single pass through the string.
And the stack itself never needs more room than the nesting depth.
Checking every possible pair by hand would be far slower.
Compilers and editors use exactly this trick to check your syntax.
One pass, one stack, and every bracket finds its partner.
That is how a simple stack keeps every string honest.
